question: According to the CAP theorem, during a network partition between nodes of a distributed system, what choice remains?

options.text: Consistency + Availability — the system is both consistent and available, just slower
options.explanation: During a partition, you cannot guarantee both consistency and availability simultaneously. If nodes can't communicate, the system either refuses to respond (CP) or responds but data may be stale (AP)

options.text: Consistency or Availability — you must sacrifice one of the two
options.explanation: In a distributed system, Partition tolerance is a given (the network WILL break). So the real choice is: CP (block requests until connection is restored, guarantee consistency) or AP (continue responding, but data may diverge)

options.text: You can choose all three — CAP only shows theoretical limits, in practice they can be bypassed
options.explanation: The CAP theorem is a mathematically proven statement, not a recommendation. During a real network partition, it's impossible to simultaneously guarantee consistency and availability. You can mitigate (tunable consistency), but not bypass the theorem

options.text: Partition tolerance or Availability — you must sacrifice one of the two
options.explanation: In a distributed system, Partition tolerance cannot be 'disabled' — network breaks are inevitable. So P is always present, and the choice is between C and A

question: Which statements about ACID and BASE are correct?

options.text: ACID guarantees that a transaction either completes entirely or not at all (Atomicity)
options.explanation: Atomicity is a key property of ACID. In a bank transfer, debit and credit are one atomic operation. If credit fails, the debit is rolled back

options.text: BASE means data will be lost on failure
options.explanation: BASE does not imply data loss. Basically Available + Soft state + Eventual consistency means the system always responds, but data may temporarily diverge between nodes. Eventual consistency — data will synchronize over time

options.text: Eventual consistency (BASE) means that after some time all nodes will have the same data
options.explanation: Eventual consistency guarantees: if writes stop, then after a finite time all replicas will converge to the same state. In practice, this takes seconds — a user updates their avatar, within 2-5 seconds all nodes see the new one

options.text: ACID systems are always slower than BASE systems
options.explanation: Not always. PostgreSQL on a single server can be faster than distributed Cassandra for simple queries. The difference shows at scale: ACID guarantees are more expensive in distributed systems due to node coordination

question: You have an e-commerce project with a product catalog (10M records), carts, and payment transactions. Which DB combination is optimal?

options.text: MongoDB for everything — flexible schema suits any data
options.explanation: MongoDB doesn't support full transactions between collections (multi-document transactions appeared in 4.0, but are slower than SQL). For payments, you need ACID. Product catalog with JOIN (product → category → reviews) maps better to SQL

options.text: PostgreSQL for catalog and transactions + Redis for carts and sessions
options.explanation: PostgreSQL provides ACID for payments, powerful JOIN for the catalog. Redis is ideal for carts (fast key-value, TTL for auto-cleaning abandoned carts) and sessions. This is the classic e-commerce combination

options.text: Cassandra for everything — scales horizontally without issues
options.explanation: Cassandra doesn't support JOIN and has limited transactions (lightweight transactions — slow). For payments, you need ACID. Cassandra is good for logs, analytics, IoT — not for transactional operations

options.text: PostgreSQL for everything — it's a universal database
options.explanation: PostgreSQL can handle it, but carts and sessions in Redis work 100x faster (0.5 ms vs 50 ms). Redis also supports TTL for auto-deleting abandoned carts. For high-load e-commerce, polyglot persistence (multiple DB types) is the standard

question: How does sharding differ from replication?

options.text: Sharding SPLITS data across servers, replication COPIES the same data to multiple servers
options.explanation: Replication: each node stores a full copy of data — scales reads and increases fault tolerance. Sharding: each node stores a portion of data — scales reads, writes, and storage volume

options.text: Sharding and replication are the same thing, just different names
options.explanation: These are fundamentally different mechanisms. Replication = copies of data. Sharding = division of data. In practice, they are combined: each shard is replicated (sharded + replicated)

options.text: Replication scales writes, sharding scales reads
options.explanation: The opposite. Replication scales reads (read from any slave), but does NOT scale writes (all writes go to master). Sharding scales both reads and writes (each shard handles its portion)

options.text: Sharding only works with NoSQL, replication only with SQL
options.explanation: Both sharding and replication work with any DB type. PostgreSQL supports replication (streaming replication) and sharding (Citus, pg_shard). MongoDB and Cassandra also support both mechanisms

question: Which statements about B-tree and Hash indexes are correct?

options.text: B-tree supports range queries (>, <, BETWEEN), hash — only exact match (=)
options.explanation: B-tree stores data in sorted order, so it efficiently handles ranges and sorting. A hash index only knows 'key exists' or 'key doesn't exist' — for > or < it would need to scan all records

options.text: Hash index is faster than B-tree for exact matches (=)
options.explanation: Hash index works in O(1) for exact matches, B-tree — in O(log N). For lookups by exact value (email, id), a hash index can be faster. In practice, the difference is negligible for most cases

options.text: Composite index (A, B, C) works efficiently for a query WHERE B = 5
options.explanation: Composite B-tree index follows the leftmost prefix rule. Index (A, B, C) works for queries on A, A+B, A+B+C. A query on B alone cannot use this index efficiently — a separate index on B is needed

options.text: The more indexes on a table, the faster all operations become
options.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes (write amplification). Each INSERT/UPDATE must update all indexes. 10 indexes = 11 write operations instead of 1. Balance: index only columns you actually search by
